# ChatGPT for Word: what it can read, what it costs and why the add-in may be missing


By OpenTools Team


OpenAI's Word add‑in is available across ChatGPT plans, but installation, workspace access and source permissions are separate gates. Here is what it can read, why it may be missing and how shared usage affects cost.


OpenAI added Word to its ChatGPT Microsoft add‑in on September 17, putting a drafting and editing sidebar beside the document rather than requiring a round trip through a browser tab. The[release notes](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/6825453-chatgpt-release-notes) say the feature is available on every ChatGPT plan, including Free, and[Microsoft's marketplace listing](https://marketplace.microsoft.com/en-us/product/office/WA200010215) identifies OpenAI as the publisher of the one add‑in serving Word, Excel and PowerPoint. There is no separate Word‑specific ChatGPT subscription to install, but plan usage limits apply and Microsoft's listing warns that an additional purchase may be required for some access. Even after installation, an organization's settings can determine whether the sidebar appears and which ChatGPT workspace a person can use.


The practical distinction is between **where the add‑in is allowed to appear** , **which ChatGPT workspace the person enters** , and **which information that workspace can supply** . The Word sidebar can use an open document and, where permitted, connected cloud sources; it cannot automatically rummage through other local files. OpenAI's[Word setup guide](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001526-chatgpt-for-word) also names two administrative controls for managed organizations: Microsoft 365 must allow the add‑in, while the ChatGPT workspace can enable or disable Word access. A missing ribbon item, a wrong workspace and a missing source are different problems, even if all three look like “ChatGPT isn't working” to a user.


##


One installation, two permission checks


For an individual, the shortest supported path is to follow the[official marketplace listing](https://marketplace.microsoft.com/en-us/product/office/WA200010215) linked from OpenAI, install the ChatGPT add‑in, open a Word document and sign in. Microsoft's listing describes the publisher as OpenAI, LLC, says one add‑in covers Word, Excel and PowerPoint, and cautions that access can vary by plan, region, workspace settings and the Microsoft 365 environment. Searching the marketplace for a vaguely named “GPT writer” extension is therefore a poor substitute for checking the publisher on the exact listing. The supported feature is the OpenAI add‑in, not any third‑party tool that happens to promise ChatGPT inside Word.


In a managed company or school account, there are two administrative gates. If the add‑in cannot be installed or does not show in Word, the Microsoft 365 administrator needs to check whether the organization allows it. If it appears but a person cannot access the intended ChatGPT workspace,[OpenAI's installation guidance](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001526-chatgpt-for-word) directs them to confirm the signed‑in account and selected workspace, then have the ChatGPT workspace administrator inspect Word access in the ChatGPT admin console. Word access will be **enabled by default starting October 1, 2026** , but that OpenAI default is not proof that a Microsoft tenant will distribute or allow the add‑in. Organizations deciding on access should resolve both gates explicitly before assuming the default will do it for them.

##


An open document is different from a connected app


Once it is available, ChatGPT for Word can draft from notes, summarize an open document, revise selected text and adjust headings or formatting, according to[OpenAI's product guide](https://chatgpt.com/apps/word/) and[help article](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001526-chatgpt-for-word) . A user might, for example, select a recommendation paragraph and ask for a tighter version that preserves the decision and numbers. For a larger document, OpenAI suggests first asking for a proposed outline or explanation of edits; complex tables, charts and formatting may still need manual correction. This is a review workflow inside Word, not a guarantee that a generated draft or reformatted report is ready to send.


The boundary around context is easy to misstate. OpenAI says the add‑in works with the document currently open and cannot automatically read other **local files on the computer** . Its current[Word product page](https://chatgpt.com/apps/word/) also says supported connected apps can provide relevant email, files and team knowledge from sources such as Outlook, SharePoint, Google Workspace and Dropbox, subject to plan, workspace settings and the person's permissions. These statements are compatible: access to a permitted connected cloud source is different from general access to local disk. A reader who needs facts from another local file can paste the relevant text; one who has an approved connected app should still check that the right workspace and source permissions are active before assuming the content will be available.


Existing ChatGPT history does not simply follow the person into Word. The[official FAQ](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001526-chatgpt-for-word) says add‑in conversations are separate from ChatGPT conversation history, and memory and skills do not carry over. The same guidance says skills can provide reusable instructions for Word tasks. **Carryover** and **availability inside Word** are thus distinct: a user should not assume a remembered instruction or skill from a separate ChatGPT conversation will appear in the document sidebar. Plugins are not currently supported in ChatGPT for Word, while supported connected apps are a separate source‑permission route.


##


“Included on Free” does not mean unconstrained use


The[marketplace listing](https://marketplace.microsoft.com/en-us/product/office/WA200010215) says people can start for free, that usage limits apply and that an additional purchase may be required. OpenAI's[Word pricing guidance](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001526-chatgpt-for-word) describes token‑based metering at the applicable model's rates, with input, cached input and output varying by model, document size and task. That is the usage basis, **not a claim that every Free user receives a separate token invoice** : an individual's included allowance, limits and possible charges depend on the plan and billing terms. Word draws from the shared usage allowance for Codex and other premium features on plans that include them, so a long document revision may consume more available usage than a small selected‑text edit.


For organizations on eligible token‑based Enterprise agreements, OpenAI's[Enterprise rate card](https://help-lb.openai.com/en/articles/20001415-chatgpt-rate-card-enterprise-token-based-pricing) lists model‑specific input, cached‑input and output rates and describes a September 17–30 GPT‑5.6 Sol preview for Word. The card explicitly limits itself to the covered agreements; credit‑billed or other plans need their own terms. It would be misleading to take an Enterprise per‑million‑token number or a time‑limited preview and present it as the price everyone pays. For a team deciding whether to roll the add‑in out, the right check is its actual workspace billing and usage configuration, together with the Microsoft 365 deployment gate—not a generic pricing screenshot.


The privacy boundary also follows the underlying ChatGPT plan and data controls. OpenAI says Business, Enterprise and Edu workspace inputs and outputs are not used to train its models by default, while the Word add‑in's access to connected sources remains controlled by the permissions on those sources.[Microsoft's listing](https://marketplace.microsoft.com/en-us/product/office/WA200010215) further says the add‑in can read and change a document, send data over the internet, and share some data with Microsoft and OpenAI to enable the feature. That gives an organization two distinct questions: whether the add‑in may run in Word at all, and which documents or connected information its users can bring into a particular task. A reviewer should still save a copy before extensive edits and verify important figures and citations, as[OpenAI's limitations](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001526-chatgpt-for-word) advise.
